Information received since the December meeting indicates a labor market that continues to strengthen and real activity expanding at a moderate pace. Interpreted through Okun’s law (the inverse relation between unemployment and output), low unemployment points to a mildly positive output outlook, while the use of PCE inflation (the FOMC’s preferred gauge) still below 2 percent tempers the tone. The decision to keep the federal funds rate at 0.50–0.75 percent and signal only gradual increases is consistent with New Keynesian policy-rule evidence (e.g., Clarida–Galí–Gertler) and the Romer and Romer literature on real effects of unanticipated policy shocks—supporting small, data-dependent steps. The mention that business fixed investment remains soft aligns with the financial accelerator and financing-constraint literature (Bernanke–Gertler), indicating that tight external finance can restrain capex despite solid employment and improved sentiment. Market-based inflation compensation remaining low and longer-term expectations little changed is consistent with anchored expectations under the New Keynesian Phillips Curve and cost-channel evidence (Christiano–Eichenbaum–Evans; Ravenna–Walsh), implying subdued inflation pressures even as inflation has risen recently. Continued reinvestment of maturing Treasury and agency MBS supports accommodative financial conditions in line with the QE literature (which raises the monetary base and compresses term premia, but has, at best, moderate effects on real growth). Overall, these points justify a cautiously positive reading rather than a strongly upbeat one.
